title: Everybody's Favorite
part: PART THREE: THE HIGH AND THE HOLE

pages.text:
*Way to Lose #28: Forget to pass and remember to celebrate.*

Monday morning, the hallway is not a hallway. It is a parade route, and I am the float. The air feels thicker, charged with the static electricity of a hundred people trying to be cool at once. Carter Boyle is waiting by the water fountain, his phone screen glowing like a predator's eye. "One for the gram?" he asks, his smile wide and slightly too white.

I lean in. The flash pops. The noise level in the hallway spikes instantly. Kids I have never spoken to, kids whose names are just smudges in my memory, stop to stare. "Captain!" one girl shouts, pointing at my yellow armband. She says it the way you would say "fire" or "ice cream." It is a title. It is a flavor.

The morning announcements crackle over the speakers. "The Marigold Park Mud Hens took their first win of the season against the Sunnyvale Sprouts. Well played." My name is attached to it. I am not a player anymore. I am a headline.

Nia stops me at my locker. She is quiet. She looks at the photo on my phone. "It's nice to see you happy," she says softly.

I shrug, adjusting my bag. "I'm not happy, Nia. I'm winning. Happy is for people who don't have a point to make." I say it lightly. It is a joke. A deflection. But the words land heavy in the air, and Nia does not smile back. She just nods, and walks away, leaving me standing there with my phone and my new, shiny, borrowed self.
pages.image: A busy school hallway with lockers, Dani leaning in for a selfie with a boy holding a phone, other students watching and pointing, one girl standing apart looking concerned, bright fluorescent lighting.

pages.text:
Practice smells like wet grass and old cleats. Coach Gin parks the yellow bus at the edge of the field, the engine ticking as it cools. We sit inside with our legs dangling over the doors, watching the grainy, shaky footage on the bus TV. It is me.

"Rewind," Gin says. She does not turn the wheel, only tapping the remote.

The video plays. I see myself in the box, the pass coming, my foot connecting with the ball, and the net rippling. Then I see the bleachers. I see my dad jumping and the crowd roaring.

I grab the remote. "Pause. Rewind to the cheer."

Gin looks at me, her sunglasses pushed up on her silver braid. She does not blink. "What did you see in the pass before the shot?" she asks, her voice flat and calm.

I open my mouth, then close it. I try to remember the moment on the field, the ball in the air, the space, the angle. I do not remember any of it. I only remember the sound, the jump, and the noise hitting my ears like a wave of static.

"I was waiting," I say, my voice small. "I was waiting for them to shout."

Gin takes the remote back and turns off the TV. The screen goes black, reflecting my face. I look tired. I look empty.
pages.image: Inside a big blank yellow minibus, a group of young soccer players watching a screen, a woman in a yellow windbreaker sitting in the driver's seat, a girl looking at her reflection in the dark screen, dim interior lighting.

pages.text:
I skip the Strategy Log on Tuesday because I have a math quiz, and on Wednesday because I am busy being famous. My locker has turned into a shrine, covered in sticky notes from teammates and stickers from fans, and I spend all my free time curating this specific image of myself.

After practice, I sit on the bench and pull off my socks. My hand finds the index card tucked inside the right one. It is slightly creased. It is a tiny white square that feels heavier than it should.

I pull it out. I look at it. Then I put it back without reading a single word. I do not want to be reminded of the girl who loses, because I have decided to be the girl who wins.

I set the card on the blue plastic seat and stand up to stretch my hamstrings. The air is cold. The grass is dark. I keep my eyes on the field.

I walk to the water fountain. I drink. I leave the card sitting there.

It is just a small white square in the vast dark field. And I refuse to look back.
pages.image: A soccer bench on a dark field, a small white card sitting on the blue plastic seat, a girl walking away toward a water fountain, empty cleats nearby, twilight sky.

pages.text:
The Dugout Diner floor is sticky, and the air smells like burnt coffee. We sit at the counter, stirring terrible milkshakes that are thick, sweet, and cloying. Ahmed leans across the table, his spoon clinking hollowly against the glass. "Can I go back to not passing?" he asks.

I look at him. He is serious. "Depends who's watching," I say.

The words hang in the air, heavy and wrong. I hear how they sound, like a rule I am making up on the fly to keep him useful. Ahmed stops stirring. He looks at the shake, then at the spoon. He says nothing, just pushes the spoon away so the liquid sloshes against the glass.

The diner is quiet, except for the other players laughing at a joke I missed. They are not laughing at me. They are laughing at the milkshake. I am not part of the laugh. I am the punchline.
pages.image: A diner counter with sticky surfaces, a boy in a soccer uniform looking down at a milkshake, a girl sitting next to him looking uncomfortable, other kids in the background laughing, harsh fluorescent lighting.

pages.text:
The garage is blindingly bright because my dad has hung a banner. It is hand-painted, the letters wobbly and red paint smeared until it looks like a scream. "MUD HENS! 1 WIN!" it proclaims.

Abuela stands on a step stool, drawing a small number in the corner. "9-12," she says without looking at me. She is focused on the line. "Next year," she adds, "we need a bigger banner. The ducks will need to see it."

I grin, showing the reporter from the free weekly paper my teeth. I flash my armband. "We just decided to be winners," I say with total authority.

Behind me, in the shadow of the car, Priya stands. She holds her gloves, staring at the floor. Her face is pale, her eyes wide, trying to make herself small.

I do not see her. My eyes are fixed on the camera lens, then on the banner. I am not looking at the girl who caught the ball in the air and saved us from ourselves. I am not looking at the person who is starting to disappear.
pages.image: A garage interior with a car, a hand-painted blank red cloth banner hanging on the wall, a girl grinning for a camera, another small girl standing in the shadow near the car looking down at the floor, bright daylight coming through the open door.
